In February 2025, Aly Coyle became the 100th person in Northern Ireland to donate a kidney to a stranger, saving the life of a 6‐year‐old boy living in England (Watson 2025). Aly is not alone—it is estimated that more than 1,000 altruistic (i.e., non‐directed) kidney donations have occurred in the United Kingdom and ∼4000 in the United States between 2001 and 2022 (Busari and Garba 2022). Why would these donors choose to help a person they do not know and will likely never meet?

Extraordinary altruism, also termed costly altruism, extreme altruism, or unusual altruism, refers to selfless acts directed to a distant other that significantly exceed normal expectations of helping and often involve risks or significant cost to the altruists themselves (e.g., Marsh et al. 2014; Oliner and Oliner 1988; Rhoads et al. 2023). This includes spontaneous altruistic acts, such as saving a stranger from drowning, as well as deliberate, calculated acts, such as donating a kidney to a stranger or donating substantial portions of one's salary to charity. When asked about their motivations, these altruists describe a range of influences, from religious and faith‐based commitments to explicitly articulated utilitarian moral frameworks emphasizing the maximization of overall welfare (MacFarquhar 2015)

A growing body of research has aimed to understand what distinguishes these extraordinary altruists from the rest of us. In a seminal study, Marsh et al. (2014) found that non‐directed kidney donors were uniquely sensitive to fearful facial expressions, a difference reflected in heightened amygdala responses to fear but not to other emotions. More recent studies have also found that altruistic kidney donors experience greater self‐other overlap in neural representations of pain and threat (Brethel‐Haurwitz et al. 2018), show reduced self‐other discounting (Vekaria et al. 2017), and differ from non‐altruist controls in their beliefs about the fundamental good of humanity (Amormino et al. 2022).

Research into extraordinary altruism has also expanded to incorporate other organ donors (e.g., liver donation; Rhoads et al. 2023), participants in SARS‐CoV‐2 human challenge trials (Rose et al. 2021), humanitarian aid workers (Rhoads et al. 2023), Carnegie Hero Medal recipients (Rand and Epstein 2014), those who have engaged in heroic acts of rescue (Rhoads et al. 2023), and those who pledged to donate large portions of their income to effective charities (Wilks et al. 2024). Echoing the results with non‐directed kidney donors, these groups also appear to differ in moral values (Amormino et al. 2022; Walker and Frimer 2007; Wilks et al. 2024) moral motivation (Rand and Epstein 2014), personality traits (Matsuba and Walker 2004), and a range of cognitive capacities (Wilks et al. 2024).

While we now know much more about what characterizes extraordinary altruism in adults, far less is known about its developmental origins. What might this altruistic motivation look like in childhood? Children cannot choose to donate their kidneys or direct large sums of money to charity. But they can choose not to eat animals. And some do, even when they are raised by families who eat meat—a choice referred to as independent vegetarianism (Hussar and Harris 2010). We see fundamental commonalities between this choice and other forms of extraordinary altruism.

First, research suggests that independently vegetarian children are particularly motivated by animal welfare when asked about their diet, even more so than vegetarians raised in vegetarian families (Hussar and Harris 2010). It's not that these children dislike the taste of meat, or think it's unhealthy—instead they typically think eating meat is morally wrong. Second, this choice can come at a personal cost. These children are giving up a food they may enjoy eating. Relatedly, there is evidence that vegetarians (Minson and Monin 2012), including childhood vegetarians (Loarte Castro 2023), experience discrimination for their choices. Finally, this decision is unusual—while many children express high levels of moral concern for animals (Caviola et al. 2025; Hussar and Harris 2018; McGuire et al. 2023, 2026; Paruzel‐Czachura et al. 2024; Wilks et al. 2021), very few make the decision to stop consuming them.

There is surprisingly little research explicitly examining vegetarianism in children. Most work focuses on nutritional outcomes for vegetarian children (Schürmann et al. 2017) and traits associated with vegetarianism in adulthood (see Rosenfeld 2018; Ruby 2012 for reviews). Moreover, while extensive research has examined children's moral development in general (see Bloom 2013; Brownell 2013; Hepach and Warneken 2018 for review), to our knowledge, only two studies have examined this case of what we see as extraordinarily altruistic motivation in childhood (i.e., independent vegetarianism). Hussar and Harris (2010, 2018) examined the beliefs and moral judgments of independently vegetarian children (6–12 years). The authors find that, compared to family and non‐vegetarian children, independent vegetarians express more concern for animal welfare when explaining their own diet choices, but that all three groups saw meat consumption as a personal choice (Hussar and Harris 2010). In another study, all three groups made similar moral judgments about harm to animals—viewing it as more morally wrong than the equivalent harm to a familiar person (e.g., a sibling; Hussar and Harris 2018). This research pioneered the study of independent vegetarianism in children and gives important insights into how these children think about meat consumption and harm to animals. However, it does not tell us about the characteristics of independent vegetarians—that is, what kind of traits might be associated with this decision. Echoing research with extraordinary altruism in adults (e.g., Rhoads et al. 2023), that is the focus of our project.

The cognitive reflection test (Frederick 2005) measures an individual's tendency to override an intuitive response and engage in reflection when answering questions. Cognitive reflection has been linked to prosocial motivations. For example, people higher in cognitive reflection are more likely to choose socially efficient distribution methods rather than those that improve their own relative shares (i.e., increasing overall funds rather than funds for themselves; Capraro et al. 2017). Moreover, past work has shown that similar traits, such as active open‐minded thinking and need for cognition, are higher in people who have taken the Giving What We Can 10% pledge to donate at least 10% of their income to effective charity (Wilks et al. 2024). As such, we predict that independently vegetarian children will be higher in cognitive reflection than family and non‐vegetarian children.

Past work has shown that the ability to recognize fearful faces sets apart extraordinary altruists—both non‐directed kidney donors (Marsh et al. 2014) and Giving What We Can pledgers (Wilks et al. 2024)—from the general public. Moreover, accurate identification of fearful faces, but not other faces, is predictive of prosocial behavior in experimental tasks (Marsh et al. 2007). In line with this, we predict that children who are independently vegetarian will be more accurately able to identify fearful faces than family and non‐vegetarians.

Disgust sensitivity is an individual's sensitivity to stimuli that commonly evoke disgust responses (Haidt et al. 1994). Developmental research shows that disgust sensitivity appears to emerge by age five (Rottman 2014). Research with adults finds clear links between meat avoidance and disgust sensitivity (Becker and Lawrence 2021)—though the direction of this effect remains unclear (Becker et al. 2022; Buttlar and Walther 2022). However, to our knowledge, no research has explicitly linked vegetarian diet and disgust in childhood. Nonetheless, we predict that independently vegetarian children will be more disgust sensitive than family and non‐vegetarians.

Our tendency to feel compassion and empathy for others is frequently related to prosocial behavior (Batson et al. 2007; Leiberg et al. 2011), though this relationship is not always consistent (Jordan et al. 2016; Preylo and Arikawa 2008; Wilks et al. 2024). However, research with children shows that they form strong connections with animals (Hawkins and Williams 2017), and one study found that children with pets were more empathetic than those without (Vidović et al. 1999). Moreover, independently vegetarian children cite moral reasons for not eating meat, and children generally report that it is wrong to harm animals because they are vulnerable (Hussar and Harris 2018). As such, we predict that independent vegetarians will be higher in empathy and compassion than family and non‐vegetarians.

SDO is a measure of an individual's preference for hierarchy within a social system (Pratto et al. 1994). Many studies with adults have linked veganism to lower rates of SDO (Allen et al. 2000; Braunsberger et al. 2021; Hodson and Earle 2018; Singer et al. 2015). Moreover, higher levels of SDO are related to other hierarchical worldviews such as racism, homophobia and, crucially, speciesism (Caviola et al. 2019). Finally, prior work shows that Giving What We Can pledgers are lower in SDO than the general population (Wilks et al. 2024). While research on SDO in children is limited, existing studies find positive links between SDO and empathy (Cadamuro et al. 2022). As such, we predict that independently vegetarian children will be lower in SDO than family or non‐vegetarians.

Speciesism is the tendency to assign moral worth based on species category (e.g., human), particularly prioritize humans over non‐human animals. Speciesism has been linked to a range of hierarchical worldviews, such as SDO and homophobia in adults (Caviola et al. 2019). Research also shows that children are generally less speciesist than adults (Henseler Kozachenko and Piazza 2021; Marshall et al. 2025; McGuire et al. 2023; Paruzel‐Czachura et al. 2024; Wilks et al. 2021). In line with this, we predict that independently vegetarian children will be lower in speciesism than family and non‐vegetarians.

We recruited adult participants from the United States via social media and snowball recruitment, targeting general pages and vegetarian‐oriented communities (e.g., Facebook, Twitter/X, Reddit). A power analysis revealed that to achieve 0.95 power and detect a medium effect size (f = 0.25) with an alpha of 0.05, a sample of N = 252 (84 per cell) was recommended (G*Power; Faul et al. 2007). A total of 681 adult participants accessed the survey. Two hundred and six were excluded for not completing the survey in full (stopping between consent and final questions), and 54 were excluded for completing most of the survey, but not specifying their diet information. Another 36 participants were removed from the survey for not meeting residency criteria (i.e., the United States).

Our sample was comprised of more female (88%) than male (12%) participants in the independent and family vegetarian groups, which is reflective of higher rates of female vegetarianism found in the general population (e.g., Pfeiler and Egloff 2018; Rosenfeld 2018). The majority of participants were white (82.1%). The rest of the sample identified as multi‐racial (7.0%), other (2.9%), Indian (2.9%), Hispanic (2.3%), Asian (1.8%), Black (0.8%), and not reported (0.3%). As is typical of online samples, our sample skewed more non‐religious (83.8%) and more liberal than the typical population, with an average score of 7.4 on a Likert scale from 1 (very conservative) to 9 (very liberal).
Cognitive reflection (Thomson and Oppenheimer 2016)
Identification of fearful faces (Adapted from Marsh et al. 2007)

This was measured as part of a larger emotion recognition task. Participants saw 16 forward facing images from the Radboud Faces Database (Langner et al. 2010), which comprised four images of four emotions: happy, angry, disgusted, and scared. Participants were asked to identify which of the four emotions was displayed. Responses were scored as correct or incorrect.
Disgust sensitivity (Olatunji et al. 2007)
Empathy and compassion (Jordan et al. 2016)
Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) (Ho et al. 2015)
Speciesism (Caviola et al. 2019)

In line with our preregistration, we conducted a multinomial logistic regression including all six personality/cognitive scales, political orientation, and religiosity as predictors and childhood diet status (independent compared to family and non‐vegetarian) as the outcome measure. We also included sex as a predictor, given the high rates of vegetarian women in the general population (Pfeiler and Egloff 2018; Rosenfeld 2018). All continuous variables were mean‐centered.

In Study 1, we find no differences between family and independent vegetarians, but we do find a number of differences between vegetarians and to non‐vegetarians. With all participants included and controlling for demographics we found that independent and family vegetarians were lower in speciesism than non‐vegetarians, and that independent (but not family) vegetarians were higher in empathy/compassion, while no other traits were predictive. In a full regression model including all traits, speciesism remained a significant predictor, whereas empathy/compassion did not. Here too we found that sex was a predictor, with females more likely to be vegetarian than males. This likely reflects vegetarianism being more prevalent in females in the general population (Pfeiler and Egloff 2018; Rosenfeld 2018).

We also examined the role of dietary motivation, with independent vegetarians reporting higher rates of animal welfare motivation than family vegetarians, consistent with past research (Hussar and Harris 2010). Independent vegetarians were also more likely to cite convenience and less likely to cite social factors than family vegetarians. Finally, in exploratory analyses, we revealed that morally motivated vegetarians were higher in empathy/compassion and lower in both SDO and speciesism, and that this persisted regardless of whether we included or excluded current vegetarians from the retrospective non‐vegetarian category.

Nine children were excluded for reasons such as parental interference (N = 3), voluntary withdrawal midway through the survey (N = 1), environmental distractions (N = 2), or failure to meet age or country of residence criteria, which was unknown until after the study's completion (N = 3). This left a final sample of 236 children (M Age = 9.39 years, Age Range = 8–11 years, SD = 1.03). Unlike the adult sample, there was an even split among sex (female = 53%; male = 47%), contrasting with higher rates of vegetarianism among females in the general population (Pfeiler and Egloff 2018; Rosenfeld 2018).

Parents completed demographic questions about their child, including a question confirming their child's diet. In addition, parents also completed a short survey about their parenting style. The survey was a subset of five items from the parenting practices questionnaire (Robinson et al. 1995). Parents were asked to rate how often they exhibit this behavior with their child on a 5‐point Likert scale ranging from Never (1) to Always (5). We selected items which capture reasoning, induction, and democratic participation to best capture parents’ encouragement of children's free and autonomous thought. For example, “I help my child to understand the impact of their behavior by encouraging my child to think about the consequences of his/her actions.” Reliability for this scale was acceptable (α = 0.70).

A growing body of research has aimed to characterize extraordinary altruists—people who engage in costly altruistic acts to benefit distant others (Amormino et al. 2022; Brethel‐Haurwitz et al. 2018; MacFarquhar 2015; Marsh et al. 2014; Vekaria et al. 2017). To date, this research has mostly focused on adults. We examine one possible expression of extraordinarily altruistic motivation in children: the decision to stop eating meat while being raised in a meat‐eating family (i.e., independent vegetarianism). Employing a retrospective adult sample (adults who adhered to the relevant diet category during childhood; Study 1) and a developmental sample (8–11‐year‐olds; Study 2) of American participants, we investigated what might differentiate independently vegetarian children from family vegetarian and non‐vegetarian children. We examined whether these three groups differed on six cognitive and personality measures: empathy/compassion, disgust sensitivity, cognitive reflection, fearful facial recognition, SDO, and speciesism. We found a number of measures that differentiated vegetarians from non‐vegetarians. However, against our key prediction, we did not identify any differences between family and independent vegetarians. We explore possible explanations for this.

Contrasting this, it may be that we missed a particular source of social influence. We assumed that independent vegetarians acted outside of the norm when deciding to become vegetarian because it was not modeled by their immediate family. However, it is also possible it was modelled by extended family members, peers, or on social media—all of which are particularly influential to young people (Tolbert and Drogos 2019; Wallis and Loy 2021). Future work could map social networks more thoroughly to better understand the role of social influence.

Another interpretation is that the relationship between our diet and values is bidirectional. That is, while many people become vegetarian because they have certain values (e.g., they care about animals), being a vegetarian might also change one's values (e.g., increase the amount that they care for animals). Under this view, becoming vegetarian for any reason might change your values and beliefs, which could explain why we found few differences between independent and family vegetarians in either sample. It also aligns with the self‐reported dietary motivation: independent and family vegetarians cited animal welfare at similar rates in the child sample, while independent vegetarians were more likely than family vegetarians to cite animal welfare in the adult sample. That is, people may become more motivated by animal welfare and less motivated by other reasons over time. This perspective is supported by both dissonance‐based accounts (the Meat Paradox; Bastian et al. 2012; Gradidge et al. 2021; Loughnan et al. 2010), as well inference‐based accounts (Self‐perception Theory; Bem 1972). While we cannot distinguish the specific mechanisms with our data, the bidirectional account seems plausible and is an important topic for future research.

While we found no differences between vegetarian groups, we did find that both vegetarian groups (family and independent) differed from non‐vegetarians on a range of measures, though these results were predominantly contained to the adult sample. First, we find robust evidence that childhood vegetarians are lower in speciesism than non‐vegetarians, reflecting findings in the existing literature with adult (Dhont and Ioannidou 2024; Leach et al. 2022). However, it is worth noting that, in the developmental sample, only family vegetarians were lower in speciesism than non‐vegetarians, while independent vegetarians did not reach the threshold for significance. It is unclear if this an issue of power or whether other demographic factors (e.g., religiosity) simply play a more prominent role.

We also found that childhood vegetarians scored higher on empathy/compassion. These findings support links between empathy and altruistic motivation, for which evidence is currently ambivalent (Amormino et al. 2022; Jordan et al. 2016; Rhoads et al. 2023; Wilks et al. 2024). In this sample, we also find evidence that vegetarians are higher in disgust sensitivity and lower in SDO. However, this pattern only emerged when we excluded participants who were raised eating meat but were vegetarian at the time of completing the survey (i.e., they were classified as meat eaters, despite currently having a vegetarian diet), and did not reliably persist when other traits were included in our models. As such, while the relationship is there, other factors may be stronger predictors. Nonetheless, our findings mirror the existing literature suggesting high disgust sensitivity and low SDO among meat avoiders (Becker et al. 2022; Becker and Lawrence 2021; Rosenfeld 2018), as well as extending work that has previously linked speciesism to other prejudices, such as SDO (Caviola et al. 2019; Dhont et al. 2016). Interestingly, it also contrasts with a body of work linking pathogen avoidance to higher social dominance orientation and other measures of conservativeness (Terrizzi et al. 2013).

We also note a number of traits in which we find no differences between groups. This reflects similarities between independent, family, and non‐vegetarian children in past literature. For example, Hussar and Harris (2010) find that all three groups think about meat eating as a personal choice, while Hussar and Harris (2018) find that all three diet groups judge harm to humans and animals in similar ways. Here, we found no differences in the ability to identify fearful faces. This contrasts with existing literature, which has found that the ability to identify fearful facial expressions is higher in non‐directed kidney donors (Marsh et al. 2014) and charitable pledgers (Wilks et al. 2024). Specific task differences may explain this result (i.e., Marsh and colleagues used a different task, while Wilks and colleagues used the same task with additional facial expressions). Indeed, participants scored quite highly overall and internal consistency was low, suggesting that the task may have been too easy. However, another potential explanation for this null is that the connection between recognizing certain emotions and altruistic motivation is target specific; the ability to better acknowledge the fear or suffering of non‐human animals would be a more predictive indicator of altruistic motivation and behavior toward animals. It would be good to replicate this with an improved measure before strong conclusions are drawn.

We also found no group‐level differences on measures of cognitive reflection. This contrasts past work finding that Giving What We Can pledgers are higher in related traits such as actively open‐minded thinking and need for cognition (Wilks et al. 2024). Importantly, Giving What We Can focuses on effective giving, thus it is plausible that these pledgers would score higher on measures related to reasoning and logic than other groups of extraordinary altruists. Finally, in Study 2 we found no evidence that parenting style was related to children's dietary choices. This contrasts with prior work showing that adults raised by egalitarian parents with non‐authoritarian parenting styles were more likely to engage in extraordinary altruism (Oliner and Oliner 1988). Again, in both of these cases, we recommend further research explores the nuances of these relationships.

Our investigation is premised on the idea that there is a moral motivation underpinning independent vegetarianism. As such, we also compared vegetarians who cited moral reasons (i.e., animal welfare) as the primary motivator for their diet to all other participants. Across both studies, morally motivated vegetarians were lower in SDO and speciesism and, in the adult sample, higher in empathy/compassion. This is similar to the previously discussed findings, though it suggests a more meaningful role of SDO. Notably, other work has linked vegan diets to lower rates of SDO and similar traits (e.g., right wing authoritarianism; Hodson and Earle 2018), suggesting that this nonhierarchical worldview may be particularly salient for vegetarians who are morally motivated.

Finally, some methodological limitations should be acknowledged in addition to those discussed earlier. First, we worked with a sample of American participants. Research with adults has shown that different values underpin vegetarian motivations across countries (e.g., Ruby et al. 2013), thus the pattern of results identified here may not persist in other cultural contexts. We also adapted validated adult scales for children, which may partially explain the largely null results in Study 2. Employing scales developed for children would be an important next step, such as the child CRT‐D scale (Young and Shtulman 2020) and the child SDO‐6 scale (Cadamuro et al. 2022)—both of which were published after our study was preregistered and data collection had begun.

We set out to understand extraordinary altruistic motivation in childhood, by examining how independent vegetarians differed from family and non‐vegetarians. We did not capture any traits that set apart independent vegetarians from family vegetarians, suggesting that the choice to become vegetarian independently may not be a helpful proxy for extraordinarily altruistic motivation. However, we did identify a number of factors that separate vegetarians from meat eaters in childhood, namely speciesism, SDO, and empathy and compassion—though these results were primarily found in the retrospective adult sample. This adds new data to the small body of literature explicitly examining independent vegetarianism in childhood (Hussar and Harris 2010, 2018), identifying traits that characterize both independent and family vegetarians.
